steps.name: https-prod
steps.where: verify (permission_callback). It is a transport precondition decided before any body work, and its only possible outcomes are pass or fail — exactly what permission_callback can express. docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md line 45 names permission_callback = apollo_wa_verify_webhook as the owner of the pipeline, so step 1 starts there.
steps.http: 401 (generic deny, identical body/shape to every other auth denial)
steps.notes: is_ssl(). Lab escape without inventing an option: wp_get_environment_type() !== 'production' (WP core 5.5+) OR a localhost/127.0.0.1 host check — do NOT add an apollo_wa_allow_http option, it is not in registry.options.keys and this run may not touch the registry beyond webhook pct fields. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy is_ssl() is false even on a real https hit; if apollo.rio.br sits behind nginx, also accept strtolower($_SERVER['HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO'] ?? '') === 'https' (spoofable, but HMAC is the actual gate, so this is cosmetic). No constant, no option, no header of ours.

steps.name: read-php-input-raw
steps.where: verify. MUST be here and nowhere else: the exact byte string hashed at step 5 is the same string measured at step 9 and decoded at steps 8/10. Reading the body a second time inside handle() would risk verifying one body and handling another — the classic signature-bypass. Cache it in per-request state at this point.
steps.http: pass-through (no status of its own — an empty or truncated body simply cannot produce a matching HMAC and dies at step 5)
steps.notes: Prefer $request->get_body(): WP_REST_Server::serve_request() already populated it from file_get_contents('php://input'), so it is the same raw bytes the SSOT asks for and survives SAPIs where php://input is not re-readable. Fall back to file_get_contents('php://input') if get_body() is empty. Do NOT call $request->get_json_params() / get_params() yet — SSOT line 46: 'JSON parse AFTER verify'. Store as $this->state[ spl_object_id($request) ]['raw'].

steps.name: require-hmac-header-401
steps.where: verify. Pure fail-closed auth precondition; SSOT line 47 says '401, log, stop'.
steps.notes: Header X-Webhook-Hmac, read via $request->get_header('x-webhook-hmac') (WP_REST_Request::canonicalize_header_name() makes case and underscore/dash irrelevant). null or '' → deny. Also deny HERE, before any hashing, if the secret is unusable: $secret = (string) Apollo_Waha_Options::get('apollo_wa_hmac_key',''); if ('' === $secret || strlen($secret) < 32) deny — registry security.hmac_min_bytes = 32. Never compute an HMAC with an empty key (an attacker who knows the key is empty can forge trivially).

steps.name: allowlist-sha512-401
steps.where: verify. Pass/fail only. Registry webhook.pipeline[3] and docs line 48: 'Algorithm allowlist: only sha512. Else 401.'
steps.notes: Header X-Webhook-Hmac-Algorithm. Allowlist is the single literal 'sha512'; compare strtolower(trim($header)) === 'sha512' so a 'SHA512' variant does not cause an outage (hex/name casing is not a security property). The server NEVER uses this value to select an algorithm — sha512 is hardcoded at step 5 — so this step is a conformance check, not a crypto control. Missing-header behaviour: see ruling 1.

steps.name: hash_hmac-sha512 + hash_equals
steps.where: verify. This is the authentication decision itself; it belongs in permission_callback by definition, and nothing downstream may run before it passes.
steps.notes: $computed = hash_hmac('sha512', $raw, $secret) → 128 lowercase hex chars. Compare hash_equals($computed, strtolower(trim($header))) — never ===, never == (SSOT 'Does not count as security' table). hash_equals arg order: known-good first. Requires Apollo_Waha_Options, which is NOT in class-plugin.php's loader — add the same guard class-client.php already uses, at the top of class-webhook.php (the only file this run may edit): if ( ! class_exists('Apollo_Waha_Options', false) ) { require_once APOLLO_WAHA_DIR . 'inc/class-options.php'; }. This is a guarded in-plugin require, not an mu/force-load, so never[] is intact. Never write $raw, the header, or the key to error_log.

steps.name: timestamp-window-300s-401
steps.where: verify. Pass/fail replay bound; must run before the dedupe ledger is consulted so a stale request never gets a transient written for it.
steps.notes: Header X-Webhook-Timestamp is unix MILLISECONDS (registry webhook.headers, docs line 18). $now_ms = (int) round( microtime(true) * 1000 ); deny when abs( $now_ms - (int) $ts ) > 300000. Use time()/microtime() (UTC) — never current_time(), which is site-local and would shift the window by the WP timezone offset. Missing or non-numeric header → deny. abs() so a far-future clock also fails, not just a stale one.

steps.name: transient-apollo_wa_hook_{id}-ttl-10min-200-empty-if-replay
steps.where: SPLIT — decided in verify, emitted by handle. permission_callback can only pass or fail, so it can never produce a 200-empty; but the step sits at position 7, ahead of 8 and 9, so it cannot simply be deferred wholesale to the handler without inverting SSOT order. Concrete resolution: verify() does the get_transient() lookup at position 7 and, on a hit, does NOT return — it sets state['replay'] = true and CONTINUES evaluating steps 8 and 9. A replayed request with a wrong session still 401s; a replayed oversized body still 413s; ordering is preserved exactly. verify() then returns true, and handle() checks the replay flag FIRST and returns 200 with an empty body without dispatching step 10. Do not short-circuit verify at step 7 — that would skip 8 and 9 for replays and reorder the pipeline.
steps.http: 200-empty on a hit; pass-through on a miss
steps.notes: Key: 'apollo_wa_hook_' . md5( $id ) — prefix is registry webhook.transient_prefix; hashing the variable part keeps the resulting _transient_ option name inside the ~172-char option_name budget and stops a client header from choosing arbitrary option names (deviation from the literal {id} in the SSOT, same prefix contract). TTL: 10 * MINUTE_IN_SECONDS. State carrier between verify and handle: private array $state keyed by spl_object_id($request) — WP_REST_Server::dispatch() hands the SAME WP_REST_Request instance to permission_callback and callback. Do NOT use $request->set_param() (it injects a fake field into the very payload step 10 reads) and do NOT use a plain static bool (rest_do_request() can dispatch more than once per PHP process). handle() must fail closed with 401 when no state row exists for the request. $id source when the header is absent: ruling 2. WHEN the transient is written: ruling 3 (after the handler succeeds, in step 10). This is an idempotency ledger mandated by SSOT step 7, not a page cache — never[] 'transients-as-page-cache' is not engaged.

steps.name: session-name-must-match-option
steps.where: verify. It is an authorization decision (SSOT status table: bad session → 401), so it belongs with the other denials; and keeping it in verify means handle() can never be reached by a foreign-session payload, which keeps any future code added to handle safe by construction. This is also the first point where JSON parsing is legal (SSOT line 46: parse AFTER verify — meaning after the HMAC at step 5, not after the whole callback).
steps.notes: $data = json_decode( $raw, true ); deny unless is_array($data) AND (string) ( $data['session'] ?? '' ) === (string) Apollo_Waha_Options::get( 'apollo_wa_session', 'apollo' ). Apollo_Waha_Options::DEFAULTS already carries 'apollo_wa_session' => 'apollo', so the default is honoured with no extra fallback logic. Envelope note: WAHA sends { event, session, payload } with session at the TOP level (payload.name repeats it for session.status) — the SSOT phrase 'payload.session' means the session field of the decoded request body, not $data['payload']['session']. Plain === is correct: the session name is not a secret, hash_equals buys nothing. Invalid JSON lands here as a deny (non-array → no session → 401). Cache $data in state so step 10 does not decode twice. Docs line 54 says 'drop', the status table says 401 — use 401 with the same generic body.

steps.name: body-max-256kb-413
steps.where: verify. permission_callback can legally emit 413: a WP_Error returned from it is converted by WP_REST_Server::dispatch() via error_to_response(), which honours the 'status' in the error data. Keeping it in verify preserves the rule that the handler is only ever entered by a fully vetted request.
steps.notes: strlen( $raw ) > 262144 (256 * KB_IN_BYTES) → new WP_Error( 'apollo_wa_webhook_too_large', '', array( 'status' => 413 ) ). Measure the raw string with strlen() (bytes), never mb_strlen(), and never trust the client-supplied Content-Length header. Note the deliberate consequence of the SSOT position: an UNSIGNED oversized body gets 401 (from step 3/5), not 413 — only a caller who proved it holds the key ever learns 413. See ruling 4.

steps.name: switch-event-no-eval-no-raw-sql
steps.where: handle (the route callback). It is the only place that produces a success response, and it is where side effects belong once every gate above has passed.
steps.http: 200 on accept. 500 only if the handler itself errors (SSOT status table: WAHA retries, handlers must be idempotent). Never 401/413 from here.
steps.notes: Literal switch/match on $data['event'], restricted to the registry webhook.events allowlist [session.status, message, message.any, message.reaction, group.v2.participants]. THIS RUN: 'session.status' → do_action( 'apollo/whatsapp/session_status', $data ) — existing hook family apollo/whatsapp/*, listener already bound at Apollo_Waha_Session::hooks() line 22 with 10/1 (see ruling 5 for what that actually achieves). 'message'/'message.any' → optional debug payload store (ruling 5 / top-level notes). Every other allowlisted event → accept and ignore, still 200. FORBIDDEN here: any Apollo_Waha_Queue call or queue status write (registry webhook.never_approves_queue = true, SSOT audit checklist last line), any Apollo_Waha_Phone call, any eval/call_user_func/variable-method built from $data['event'], any $wpdb query built from body values, any register_rest_route. Write the dedupe transient at the END of this step, on the success path only (ruling 3). Return new WP_REST_Response( array( 'ok' => true ), 200 ).

rulings.question: 1. X-Webhook-Hmac-Algorithm missing entirely — does missing mean 401, given the server always computes sha512 and never lets the client choose?
rulings.recommendation: Treat missing as 401, same as present-but-wrong. Registry security.fail_closed = true and pipeline[3] is literally 'allowlist-sha512-401'; an allowlist by definition admits only values that are IN the list, and an absent value is not in it. Soften only the parts that cost nothing: compare strtolower(trim($h)) === 'sha512' so casing/whitespace never causes an outage, and log a DISTINCT internal reason code (error_log / apollo log, never the response body) so ops can tell 'algo header absent' from 'bad hmac' without the 401 leaking which check failed. Keep it as one isolated conditional so that, if the Docker lab proves a WAHA build or a proxy omits the header, flipping it to 'if present, must be sha512' is a one-line change with a comment pointing at this decision.
rulings.argument_against: Cryptographically this header is decorative: the server pins sha512 at step 5 and never reads the client's claim, so there is no downgrade or algorithm-confusion surface and rejecting on absence buys exactly zero security. What it buys instead is a new availability dependency — any WAHA version bump, any reverse proxy that drops non-standard X- headers, any future relay, and every single event 401s while the SSOT simultaneously forbids the 401 from hinting why. That failure looks identical to a wrong HMAC key, so the first debugging move will be rotating a key that was never wrong. A lenient 'present-but-wrong → 401, absent → proceed' reading is defensible and strictly more robust.
rulings.confidence: medium-high on the ruling, high that the header is security-irrelevant

rulings.question: 2. X-Webhook-Request-Id missing — dedupe with no id? Is a body/signature-derived fallback key better than skipping dedupe?
rulings.recommendation: Derive a fallback, never skip dedupe, never 401. Fallback key material = the verified HMAC hex plus the timestamp header: $id = 'sig_' . substr( hash( 'sha256', $hmac_normalized . '|' . $ts ), 0, 40 ). Rationale: the HMAC is a deterministic function of (secret, raw body), so identical bodies collide and different bodies do not, and only a holder of the key can produce one — it is a sound idempotency token. Folding in the timestamp keeps two legitimately identical payloads sent at different moments distinguishable (repeat 'session.status → WORKING' envelopes are entirely plausible and must not be swallowed as replays). Hash before use: never put the raw signature hex into a transient key, because it then lands in wp_options option_names and in any query log. Apply the same md5() wrapping to a PRESENT header too (step 7 notes) — a header is attacker-controlled text and must never choose an option name or blow the _transient_ name-length budget. Skipping dedupe entirely is the one option to reject outright: it deletes the only defence the SSOT has against replay inside the 300s window.
rulings.argument_against: A fallback silently accepts a request that is malformed per the SSOT header contract, so a real WAHA misconfiguration (or a proxy stripping the id) becomes invisible instead of loud — and if WAHA in fact always sends the id, the branch is dead code that will never be exercised or tested. It also quietly changes the dedupe SEMANTICS from delivery-identity to body-identity: two genuinely distinct deliveries that happen to carry byte-identical bodies within the same millisecond collapse into one, and the second is dropped as a 200-empty 'replay' — a silently lost event, which is the exact failure mode ruling 3 works hard to avoid. A strict 401 would surface the misconfiguration on the first event.

rulings.question: 3. WHEN is the dedupe transient written — on first sight (before handling) or after the handler succeeds?
rulings.recommendation: AFTER the handler completes without error, as the last action of step 10. The SSOT's own status table ('Handler error after auth → 500 (WAHA will retry — handlers must be idempotent)') is only coherent if a failed handle leaves NO dedupe record: otherwise the retry the doc promises would hit the transient and get a 200-empty, and the event would be permanently lost while every log line says success. Choose double-processing over silent loss. That choice is cheap here specifically because this run's handlers are trivially idempotent by construction — a do_action and an option overwrite — and because the webhook is forbidden from touching queue status (registry webhook.never_approves_queue), so a double-process cannot corrupt the join chain, which is the one place where duplication would actually hurt. Corollary: keep handle() synchronous and fast (no outbound HTTP — see ruling 5) so the success write lands within milliseconds of dispatch and the vulnerable window is tiny.
rulings.argument_against: Write-after-success is weaker exactly where dedupe is named: an attacker who captures one signed body can replay it freely inside the 300s timestamp window for as long as each attempt fails, because no ledger row is ever laid down — the protection only begins after the first success. It also does nothing for the slow-but-eventually-successful handler: if WAHA's delivery timeout fires before the response returns, the retry enters handle() concurrently with the original and nothing serializes the two. Write-on-first-sight ('claim then handle') closes both holes. An honest middle path exists — claim with a short in-flight marker (~60s TTL) before dispatch, promote it to the full 10-minute record on success, delete it on failure — and it is what I would build once real handlers have side effects; it is more machinery than this run's pipeline warrants. Separately, note that get_transient/set_transient is not compare-and-set: two simultaneous deliveries can both miss the lookup under any of these schemes (WP has no atomic transient-add API), so dedupe here is best-effort, not a lock.

rulings.question: 4. body-max-256kb sits at step 9, AFTER the HMAC at step 5. Real DoS concern, or is following SSOT order fine?
rulings.recommendation: Follow the SSOT order exactly — 413 only after HMAC, timestamp and session all pass. The DoS framing does not survive contact with the request lifecycle: by the time any line of this plugin executes, PHP has already read and buffered the entire body (post_max_size, default 8M, is enforced at the SAPI layer long before WordPress boots, and nginx client_max_body_size, default 1M, rejects bigger bodies with its own 413 before PHP is even reached). The memory is already spent; a userland size check cannot un-spend it. What it could save is the hashing, and sha512 over a few hundred KB to a few MB is sub-millisecond to low-milliseconds — nothing next to the WordPress bootstrap that already ran. Meanwhile the SSOT order buys a real property: an UNAUTHENTICATED oversized body gets 401, not 413, so a stranger cannot probe the size limit; only a caller who has proved it holds the key learns that 413 exists. Reordering would leak that for free. The genuine oversized-body control is ops — nginx client_max_body_size and post_max_size — and it does not belong in this file.
rulings.argument_against: 'Reject cheap, reject early' is a legitimate defensive instinct, and it stops being theoretical on hosts that raise post_max_size to 64M+ for media uploads: an unauthenticated attacker could then make the server HMAC 64MB per request, and the concurrency amplifies. If that is the deployment, the mitigation is a defence-in-depth OUTER bound (e.g. reject anything above a few MB before step 5) kept separate from, and not a replacement for, the SSOT 256KB check at position 9 — so the SSOT ordering and its non-leaking 401 behaviour stay intact. Given apollo.rio.br's WAHA is bound to 127.0.0.1 / a private network per registry.waha.bind, even that is belt-and-braces.

rulings.question: 5. 'session.status updates Session strip' — class-session.php may not be edited this run, on_status() is an empty stub, and the strip reads a 30s transient written by Session::ping(). What can the webhook honestly do?
rulings.recommendation: Do (A) unconditionally, and nothing else this run. (A) do_action( 'apollo/whatsapp/session_status', $data ) in the step-10 switch. What it actually achieves: the contract goes live end-to-end — the hook already exists in registry.hooks.actions, Apollo_Waha_Session::hooks() already binds on_status() to it at 10/1, so a real WAHA status event now reaches a real listener. What it does NOT achieve: the strip does not move one pixel, because on_status() is an empty method body. That is the honest, complete truth of this run and it should be stated in the registry note rather than papered over — 'event delivered to the listener; the listener is still a stub, strip updates land when class-session.php may be edited'. The full option set, with what each really buys: (A) fire the action — extension point live, strip unchanged, zero risk, zero coupling; the right answer. (B) have the webhook write Session's own ping cache directly — set_transient( 'apollo_wa_session_ping_' . md5($session), array('ok'=>true,'status'=>200,'body'=>array('status'=>$data['payload']['status'])), 30 ) — this genuinely moves the strip with no edit to class-session.php, but it reaches into another class's PRIVATE cache key and duplicates its 30s TTL constant by hand, and it changes the strip's meaning from 'WP pinged WAHA and saw this' to 'someone pushed this at us', while apollo_wa_last_ping goes stale and misreports freshness; a signed-but-stale event pins a wrong status for 30s. Reject as primary. (C) trigger an authoritative refresh — Apollo_Waha_Session::instance()->ping( true ) — no coupling, no fabrication, strip shows verified truth; but it puts a 20s-timeout outbound HTTP call inside the webhook response path, which invites WAHA's delivery timeout, a 500, and a retry storm, and it directly contradicts ruling 3's 'keep handle() fast so the success write lands quickly'. Viable only behind a throttle transient (at most one ping per N seconds) and I would not add it this run. (D) write a new option such as apollo_wa_last_status — nothing reads it (admin files are out of scope), so it achieves debug value only, and it adds a key absent from registry.options.keys, i.e. registry drift that this run's edit scope ('registry pct fields for webhook') does not authorize. Reject. For the 'message may store last payload for debug' allowance, use update_option( 'apollo_wa_last_webhook', $truncated_json, false ) called DIRECTLY rather than Apollo_Waha_Options::set(), because set() forces autoload=true for non-secret keys and would put up to 256KB of JSON into the autoloaded option set on every page load of the whole site; truncate to a few KB, strip media/base64 fields, never store the HMAC header, and gate it on WP_DEBUG or wp_get_environment_type() !== 'production' so prod does not take a DB write per inbound message.
rulings.argument_against: (A) alone means the visible outcome of this run is nil: an operator watching the session strip sees exactly what they saw before, and 'RUN 2 wired the webhook' will read as a claim unsupported by anything on screen — which is precisely the kind of gap the registry's own classification ('designed_skeleton_not_working_bridge') exists to call out. (B) is the only option that produces a visible result under this run's edit constraint, its coupling is to a key that is stable and sits one directory away, and one could argue that a WAHA-pushed status is fresher and more authoritative than a 30s-old poll — WAHA knows its own session state before WP can ask. If the operator's acceptance criterion for RUN 2 is 'the strip reacts to a real event', (B) plus a loud code comment naming the coupling is the pragmatic call, and (A) should ship alongside it either way.
rulings.confidence: high on (A); medium on rejecting (B), since it hinges on how this run's success is judged

notes:
CROSS-CUTTING FINDINGS (all verified against the files read).

1) THE 403 TRAP — the most important defect to fix. The current stub's `verify()` returns `false` (inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php:37). WP core turns a `false` permission_callback into `rest_forbidden` with `rest_authorization_required_code()`, which is 401 only when the caller is logged OUT and **403 when logged in**. So an admin testing the route from a cookie-bearing browser gets 403 today, contradicting the SSOT status table. Every deny in the new pipeline must therefore return an explicit WP_Error, never `false`: one private helper, one error code, one message, one status, e.g. `new WP_Error( 'apollo_wa_webhook_denied', __( 'Unauthorized.', 'apollo-waha' ), array( 'status' => 401 ) )`, shared by all five 401 steps (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8). Identical body, identical code, identical headers for every auth failure — that is what satisfies docs/WEBHOOK-SECURITY.md line 102, "401 must not leak 'key almost correct'", and the audit-checklist line "401 does not hint key proximity". Log the real reason internally only.

2) VERIFY OWNS 1-9, HANDLE OWNS 10 (plus the emission of 7). The alternative split — verify does 1-6, handle does 7-10 — also preserves SSOT ordering and makes the 200-empty natural, and is worth naming as the runner-up. I recommend against it because: (a) docs line 45 names permission_callback as the pipeline owner; (b) step 8 is an authorization decision (401), so it belongs with the other denials; (c) with 1-9 in verify, handle() is unreachable by any unauthenticated, foreign-session or oversized request, which makes every future line added to handle safe by construction. The one thing verify structurally cannot do is emit a 2xx — hence the flag-carry at step 7, and only at step 7.

3) 413 FROM permission_callback IS LEGAL. A WP_Error returned by a permission_callback is converted by `WP_REST_Server::dispatch()` through `error_to_response()`, which honours `array('status' => 413)` in the error data. Step 9 therefore does not need to move to the handler to emit 413.

4) STATE CARRIER. WP hands the SAME `WP_REST_Request` instance to permission_callback and to callback, so a private `array $state` keyed by `spl_object_id( $request )` is the correct carrier for {raw, data, replay, dedupe_key} between verify and handle. Not `$request->set_param()` (it injects a fake field into the payload step 10 reads). Not a plain static bool (`rest_do_request()` can dispatch more than once per PHP process). handle() must fail closed — 401 — when no state row exists for its request, in case it is ever reached without verify (`rest_pre_dispatch` short-circuits, direct calls).

5) ROUTE SURFACE UNCHANGED. `register_rest_route( 'apollo/v1', '/wa/webhook', ... )` with `'methods' => 'POST'` and `'permission_callback' => array( $this, 'verify' )` stays byte-identical. No `'args'` schema added (a schema would make WP parse/validate the body before verify runs). No second route. Namespace stays apollo/v1 — never[] intact.

6) OPTIONS AVAILABILITY. `Apollo_Waha_Options` is deliberately absent from `Apollo_Waha_Plugin::load()` (inc/class-plugin.php:33-44); it is pulled in by inc/Client/class-client.php:10-12 under a `class_exists(..., false)` guard. Load order today happens to put Client before Webhook, so the class is present — but relying on that is fragile. Repeat the identical guard at the top of inc/Webhook/class-webhook.php. That is an edit to the one permitted file, matches the established in-plugin pattern, and is not a force-load/mu require, so never[] is intact.

7) REGISTRY pct FIELDS THIS RUN MAY TOUCH (webhook-scoped only, per the operator instruction): modules[id=webhook].pct_built (15) and .code_today/.status; features[id=webhook_hmac_pipeline].pct_built (15) and .status; rest.routes.webhook.pct_built (15), .status ("registered_always_401") and .permission_callback ("verify → currently hardcodes false"); webhook.code_pct (5); moments[id=M6_webhook_hit].pct_built (5). BORDERLINE, flagging rather than assuming: security.code_pct (5) and security.note ("Current verify() hardcodes false"), layers.core_bridge, build_totals.* and summary.bottom_line all currently assert the webhook is a fail-closed stub and will be factually wrong after this run — but they are not "webhook pct fields" in the narrow sense. Get an explicit ruling before touching them. registry.hooks.actions[apollo/whatsapp/session_status].pct_built (10) is likewise outside the stated scope even though ruling 5(A) makes it half-true.

8) OUT OF SCOPE, DECLARED BUT NOT IN pipeline[]: `webhook.rate_limit` = "30 events/min/session" exists in the registry and in the docs' "HMAC does not cover" section, but it is NOT one of the ten pipeline[] entries, so it is not part of this run. When it is built, its natural position is between steps 6 and 7 (after the request is proven authentic, before the dedupe ledger is consulted), keyed per session name.

9) TRANSIENT VOLUME. With no external object cache, `set_transient()` with an expiry writes to wp_options with autoload off. At the declared 30 events/min ceiling and a 10-minute TTL that is ≤300 rows at steady state, cleaned by WP's expired-transient housekeeping. Acceptable, and it is an idempotency ledger explicitly mandated by SSOT step 7 — never[]'s "transients-as-page-cache" prohibition is not engaged.

10) KNOWN GAP IN WAHA'S OWN SCHEME, worth a code comment rather than a fix: the HMAC signs the raw body only, not the headers. X-Webhook-Request-Id and X-Webhook-Timestamp are therefore unauthenticated, so a captured valid body can be re-sent with a fresh Request-Id and a fresh (in-window) timestamp to defeat dedupe. The 300s timestamp window is the bound on that, and it is WAHA's design, not something this file can close. Documented, not solved.
